title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Testability Failure (Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics)
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200. Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Crucially, this ceiling outcome is a testability failure (non‑informative for the preregistered causal estimand) and must not be interpreted as evidence that the LLM+validator pipeline is safe in production. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle.

sections.introduction: Automating human intent → device configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency in NetOps but risks outages or policy violations when proposed changes are incorrect or misordered. Tool‑augmentation—pairing an LLM generator with deterministic validators/simulators in generate–validate–repair pipelines—has been proposed to reduce those risks. We preregistered a confirmatory paired study (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to measure whether adding a deterministic sandbox validator reduces verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistered estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline) assessed by an exact McNemar two‑sided test with paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Contributions: (1) a fully archived, deterministic preregistered paired experiment and its numerical outcomes; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the execution produced a non‑informative ceiling result; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations to make future repeats informative under the same preregistration framework.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototype reports document rapid adoption of LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, limited remediation) and emphasize evaluation and safety challenges [1,2,3]. Tool‑augmentation and divide–verify–refine architectures are widely proposed and shown to reduce constraint violations on curated tasks, but reported gains depend strongly on verifier fidelity and evaluation semantics (sampling, repair policies, generation budgeting) [4,5]. Guardrail and red‑teaming studies from adjacent domains stress adversarial calibration and ROC‑style diagnostics to capture both false negatives and false refusals; practical trade‑offs between stricter validation and operator burden remain an open empirical question [6,7]. Our work aligns with these lines by preregistering a paired causal estimand, using deterministic synthetic tasks and sandboxed validation, and archiving full validator traces to permit replay and audit.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as cand-2026-01-prereg-v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on deterministic validator SAFE labels. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar (paired_binary_analysis_v1); CI: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planned N=200 paired tasks (400 episodes) with a power plan based on an anticipated baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS multi‑device topologies and limited fields (admin, MTU, VLAN). Per‑task manifests included initial_state, expected_final_state, and explicit required_sequence constraints.

Compared pipelines. Baseline: post‑hoc scoring of the LLM candidate by the deterministic validator. Guarded: deterministic validation of the same or (in other semantics) independently generated candidate; in this execution the guarded arm performed validation only (repair_provider_trace fields are null in scoring JSONs).

Generation semantics and budget. The preregistration allowed independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task scored by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve budget (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json) so each paired episode used the identical generated candidate for both arms.

Scoring and analysis. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 produced deterministic validator outputs (validation_before/after, violation lists) that defined the binary SAFE indicator. Analysis was executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1 and produced the 2×2 contingency, exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI. All analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/*.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). 

Why the inferential test was uninformative. The preregistered paired contrast is identifiable only when the two arms can produce discordant SAFE labels. In this execution three archived facts together made discordance impossible: (A) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced a single LLM candidate per task shared by both arms (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json); (B) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate as valid (scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/ show validator.valid = true and violation_count = 0); and (C) no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs). Because identical candidates were scored identically by a deterministic validator and no repairs changed candidates, the per‑pair outcomes were mechanically concordant and McNemar’s test had no discordant pairs to evaluate, producing a degenerate inferential result.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting. The execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json). Provider audit logs recorded 200 hosted model call events; no cross‑condition cache reuse was observed.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Deterministic validator SAFE labels were observed for every confirmatory episode: baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These results are direct outputs of paired_binary_analysis_v1 and are archived in analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv.

Representative traces. Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across baseline and guarded episodes, validator.valid = true, violation_count = 0, and null repair_provider_trace fields. The archived raw response files (execution/responses/task-XXXX-shared-initial.txt) contain the exact generated configurations used by both arms.
sections.discussion:
Diagnostic synthesis. The degenerate contingency arises because the executed semantics and observed validator outputs left no possible source of arm‑level disagreement. This is a testability/design failure rather than evidence of verifier effectiveness or system safety. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate and discordant proportions; those assumptions did not hold.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats. All recommendations follow directly from the archived execution and preregistration artifacts: (1) use independent per‑arm generation when the estimand is a paired causal contrast (preregistered maximum_model_calls would be ≈400 versus the executed 200); (2) allocate and consume the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until baseline unsafe rates match power assumptions; (3) if the guarded pipeline includes repairs, archive and analyze repair_provider_trace artifacts and quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and any repair‑induced violations; (4) add a small deterministic pilot check before the full confirmatory run and abort the confirmatory test if the pilot yields ceiling/floor contingencies, then follow preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptation paths. The execution and analysis artifacts record the exact model_call trade‑offs and the null repair trace that motivate these steps (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/scoring/*.json).

Threats to validity and operational notes. The synthetic task family and validator scope (admin/mtu/vlan, single‑AS topologies) limit external validity. Deterministic validator completeness relative to production failure modes is unassessed here. Because no refusals or repairs occurred, we cannot estimate false‑refusal or repair‑utility trade‑offs from this run; those were intended to be measured in the preregistered exploratory reserve. Operational decisions should weigh the extra model‑call cost of independent draws and exploratory calibration against the inferential value required to justify automated execution in production.

Reproducibility. All artifacts required to replay and inspect the executed semantics, per‑task scoring JSONs, validator traces, and analysis outputs are archived in the bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). These permit deterministic replay of the non‑informative outcome and verification of the diagnosis above.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic validator‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This ceiling outcome is a testability failure: because identical candidates were scored identically by a deterministic validator and no repairs altered candidates, the preregistered paired causal estimand was not testable in this run. This result is non‑informative with respect to verifier efficacy and must not be interpreted as evidence that the pipeline is safe in production. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a deterministic preregistered run archived for replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the testability failure; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC estimation, and pilot checks) to enable informative repeats. Investigators seeking informative inference under the same estimand should follow the archived recommendations before re‑executing confirmatory trials.

Validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation and encoded outcomes as binary labels (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation; archived scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) contain validator traces showing validation_before/after and violation lists. Analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency, exact McNemar two‑sided test, and paired bootstrap CI (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729); analysis artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes were executed; the observed model call count reflects the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics. Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals occurred prior to the lock but were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under the post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
